title: Episode 115: Thomas Jefferson and the First Barbary War: The Shores of Tripoli
description:
When Thomas Jefferson took office as the third President of the United States in eighteen-one, the fledgling American republic faced an intolerable humiliation on the high seas. For decades, the North African Barbary states of Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli, and Morocco had seized merchant ships, captured their crews, and demanded extortionate ransom and annual tributes from Western maritime nations. European superpowers had long paid off the corsairs as an ordinary cost of business, but Jefferson refused to bow. Declaring that the young nation would pay millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute, Jefferson dispatched American warships to the Mediterranean Sea in the nation's first foreign conflict.

This is the dramatic saga of the First Barbary War: the humiliating grounding and capture of the frigate USS Philadelphia in Tripoli harbor, Stephen Decatur's audacious nighttime raid into the lion's den to burn the ship under enemy cannons, and General William Eaton's legendary five-hundred-mile march across the Libyan desert with a handful of United States Marines and Arab mercenaries to seize the fortress of Derne. Join George as he brings to life the crucible of courage that forged the American naval tradition and inspired the immortal words, 'to the shores of Tripoli.'

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we continue our journey through the American Presidency with the second chapter in the life of Thomas Jefferson. We often remember Jefferson as the philosophical architect of the Declaration of Independence, a gentleman farmer, and a passionate scholar. Yet in eighteen hundred and one, Jefferson was confronted with a crisis that demanded raw military courage and strategic daring. The corsairs of North Africa held American merchantmen hostage, demanding gold for the right to sail free waters. European empires paid the bribes, but Jefferson drew a line in the sand, launching America's first foreign war and setting the stage for one of the most daring naval exploits in human history. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CORSAIRS OF THE MEDITERRANEAN
In the late eighteenth century, the azure waters of the Mediterranean Sea were among the most treacherous maritime crossroads on Earth. For centuries, the Barbary States along the North African coast—the regencies of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, along with the independent Sultanate of Morocco—had conducted state-sponsored privateering. Their swift, armed corsair vessels darted out from fortified harbors to prey upon unprotected merchant shipping. When a vessel was seized, its cargo was confiscated, and its Christian crew and passengers were chained, marched ashore, and sold into brutal bondage. The rulers of these regencies, known as Deys, Beys, and Pashas, extorted staggering fortunes from European powers in exchange for treaties of immunity and the ransom of captured sailors.
Great Britain and France, possessing massive navies, chose cynically to pay annual tributes amounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars. It served the commercial interests of the superpowers to keep the pirates active, as it drove smaller, weaker maritime nations out of Mediterranean trade. But for the newborn United States of America, having won independence and lost the protective umbrella of the Royal Navy, American merchantmen were defenseless lambs. American ships carrying wheat, timber, and flour were routinely boarded, and by eighteen hundred, more than a hundred American sailors languished in dark North African dungeons, subjected to hard labor and despair. The fledgling United States was spending nearly twenty percent of its total federal revenue just paying ransom and tribute to keep the peace. To Thomas Jefferson, this arrangement was not diplomacy. It was an intolerable surrender of national honor and commercial sovereignty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: JEFFERSON'S DOCTRINE: MILLIONS FOR DEFENSE
Thomas Jefferson had opposed paying tribute to the Barbary pirates since the seventeen-eighties, when he served as American minister to France alongside John Adams in London. While Adams pragmatically argued that paying tribute was cheaper than building and maintaining a permanent navy, Jefferson argued with prophetic fury that buying peace only guaranteed endless extortion. He wrote that justice and respect among nations could never be purchased with gold; it had to be established with cannon shot.
When Jefferson assumed the presidency in March eighteen-one, the Pasha of Tripoli, Yusuf Karamanli, decided to test the resolve of the new American leader. Demanding an immediate payment of two hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars plus an increased annual tribute, Karamanli grew impatient when the funds were not forthcoming. On May fourteenth, eighteen-one, the Pasha ordered his soldiers to march to the American consulate in Tripoli and dramatically chop down the American flagstaff. It was an unambiguous declaration of war.
Jefferson did not hesitate. Without waiting for a formal declaration of war from Congress, he exercised his executive authority as Commander-in-Chief to dispatch a small squadron of four warships, led by the frigates President, Philadelphia, and Essex, to the Mediterranean under Commodore Richard Dale. Their orders were clear: protect American commerce, blockade the port of Tripoli, and demonstrate to the corsairs that the United States would defend its citizens by force of arms. It was the first time in American history that the United States Navy was deployed across an ocean to wage offensive combat.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE DISASTER OF THE USS PHILADELPHIA
For two long years, the American blockade of Tripoli proved frustrating and indecisive. The Mediterranean was thousands of miles from American shipyards, supply lines were painfully stretched, and the deep-draft American frigates struggled to navigate the shallow, treacherous coastal shoals where the pirate gunboats thrived. In the autumn of eighteen-three, command of the Mediterranean squadron fell to Commodore Edward Preble, an aggressive, iron-willed officer who brought new discipline and energy to the campaign.
Preble ordered the thirty-six-gun heavy frigate USS Philadelphia, commanded by Captain William Bainbridge, to enforce a tight blockade on Tripoli harbor. On October thirty-first, eighteen-three, the Philadelphia spotted a Tripolitan corsair trying to slip into the port. Bainbridge gave chase, pressing his ship forward under full sail. But in the heat of pursuit, the frigate entered uncharted waters. Suddenly, with a deafening shudder that shook the masts to their foundations, the Philadelphia ran hard aground on an unmarked reef known as the Kaliusa Shoal, just three miles outside the harbor.
Bainbridge and his crew fought desperately to free the vessel. They threw heavy cannons overboard, pumped out freshwater casks, and even chopped down the foremast to lighten the keel, but the ship remained wedged tight. Within hours, Tripolitan gunboats swarmed the stranded leviathan like wolves, raking her defenseless decks with grape and round shot. Realizing that further resistance would mean the slaughter of his crew, Bainbridge ordered the ship's magazines flooded, the guns spiked, and the colors struck. Captain Bainbridge and three hundred and seven American officers and sailors were captured and hauled into the dungeons of Tripoli. To make matters infinitely worse, high tide and heavy seas soon floated the Philadelphia free. The Tripolitans towed the prize into their inner harbor, pumped out the water, mounted heavy guns upon her decks, and prepared to turn America's own magnificent warship against Preble's fleet.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: DECATUR'S AUDACITY IN THE LION'S DEN
The capture of the Philadelphia was a catastrophic blow to American prestige and military fortunes. The Pasha now held three hundred American hostages and a warship capable of breaking any blockade. Commodore Preble knew that retaking the Philadelphia was impossible, but leaving her in pirate hands was unthinkable. The ship had to be destroyed inside the heavily defended harbor, surrounded by over one hundred coastal artillery batteries and a fleet of armed gunboats. It was considered a suicide mission.
Command of the strike was entrusted to a dashing twenty-five-year-old lieutenant named Stephen Decatur. Decatur chose to use a captured Tripolitan ketch, renamed the USS Intrepid. Because the ketch was rigged in the Mediterranean fashion, it could slip past harbor defenses without raising immediate alarm. On the night of February sixteenth, eighteen-four, Decatur sailed the Intrepid into Tripoli harbor under a pale crescent moon. Hidden below decks in suffocating heat were seventy-four American sailors and eight United States Marines armed with cutlasses, boarding pikes, and incendiary torches. Only a handful of men, dressed in traditional Maltese sailor garb, stood visible on deck, accompanied by a bilingual Sicilian pilot.
As the Intrepid drifted within hailing distance of the towering Philadelphia, the pilot calmly called out in Italian to the Tripolitan sentries, claiming they had lost their anchors in a storm and requested permission to tie up alongside the frigate until morning. The guards agreed and threw down a mooring line. The instant the two vessels touched, Decatur leaped onto the Philadelphia's deck, shouting the battle cry: 'Boarders away!' The Americans swarmed up the side like phantoms. Refusing to fire muskets to preserve the element of surprise, they engaged the stunned guards in savage hand-to-hand combat, clearing the decks in less than ten minutes without losing a single man.
Decatur's men moved with lightning precision. They carried kegs of powder and sacks of pitch into the hold, the storerooms, and the captain's cabin, lighting fuses across the vessel. The dry timber and tar erupted into a blazing inferno so rapidly that the boarding party had to leap into the Intrepid as flames licked their clothes. As the Intrepid rowed furiously away under the barrage of scores of shore guns, the Philadelphia exploded in a cataclysmic pillar of fire that illuminated the night sky. When British Admiral Lord Horatio Nelson heard of the raid, he declared it 'the most bold and daring act of the age.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MARCH ACROSS THE LIBYAN SANDS
While Decatur's raid robbed Tripoli of its prize warship, the three hundred American captives, including Captain Bainbridge, remained trapped in underground dungeons. The Pasha refused to negotiate, believing his fortress walls were impregnable from the sea. Realizing that naval bombardment alone could not force a surrender, Thomas Jefferson authorized an extraordinary, unconventional land campaign conceived by William Eaton, a former army captain and the fiery former American consul to Tunis.
Eaton's audacious plan was to exploit a dynastic civil war. The ruling Pasha, Yusuf Karamanli, had usurped the throne years earlier by murdering his older brother and sending his eldest brother, Hamet Karamanli, into exile in Egypt. Eaton proposed finding Hamet in Egypt, raising an army under his name, and marching five hundred miles across the unforgiving Libyan desert to strike Tripoli from the rear, restoring Hamet to power in exchange for peace and the unconditional release of the American prisoners.
In early eighteen-five, Eaton tracked down Hamet near Alexandria. To spearhead the overland expedition, Eaton assembled an improbable coalition: eight United States Marines commanded by First Lieutenant Presley O'Bannon, about forty European mercenaries, and four hundred Arab bedouin cavalry and camel drivers. On March eighth, eighteen-five, this ragged army set out into the desolate wastes of the Libyan Desert. The five-hundred-mile march was a harrowing ordeal. Water holes were frequently dry, rations dwindled to a handful of rice per day, and the Arab mercenaries mutinied multiple times, threatening to murder Eaton and the Marines. Each time, Eaton and Lieutenant O'Bannon stood shoulder-to-shoulder with drawn swords and fixed bayonets, staring down the mutineers through sheer force of will. After fifty days of brutal desert march, Eaton's parched vanguard crested the rocky hills overlooking the fortified port city of Derne, the second-largest stronghold in the Regency of Tripoli.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BATTLE OF DERNE: TO THE SHORES OF TRIPOLI
Derne was defended by a garrison of eight hundred experienced Ottoman soldiers, entrenched behind stone ramparts and heavy brass cannons. When Eaton sent a courier offering generous terms if the governor surrendered without bloodshed, the governor returned a curt, famous reply: 'My head or yours.'
On the morning of April twenty-seventh, eighteen-five, three American naval vessels—the Nautilus, the Argus, and the Hornet—arrived offshore precisely on schedule, opening a ferocious naval bombardment against the city's harbor batteries. While the naval guns battered the seaward fortifications, Eaton divided his meager force into two assault columns. Hamet Karamanli's cavalry swept around to attack the governor's palace from the southwest, while William Eaton, Lieutenant Presley O'Bannon, and their eight Marines launched a direct frontal assault on the main harbor battery.
Charging across an open plain under withering musket and grape fire, Eaton was shot through the wrist, but refused to stop. Lieutenant O'Bannon and his Marines led the desperate charge up the parapets, breaching the walls with cold steel. In vicious hand-to-hand fighting, the Marines captured the enemy battery, swung the captured Turkish cannons around, and turned them against the fleeing defenders. By four in the afternoon, the town had fallen. Lieutenant O'Bannon climbed the heights of the harbor fortress and raised the Stars and Stripes above a captured foreign stronghold for the very first time in United States history. In gratitude for their heroic liberation of his territory, Hamet Karamanli presented Lieutenant O'Bannon with a jewel-encrusted, curved Mameluke sword. That iconic weapon became the pattern for the dress swords carried by every United States Marine Corps officer to this day, and the battle forever enshrined the words 'to the shores of Tripoli' in the Marine Corps Hymn.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: LEGACY OF THE FIRST FOREIGN WAR
The stunning fall of Derne, combined with the tightened naval blockade and the threat of an immediate overland march on Tripoli itself, shattered the resolve of Pasha Yusuf Karamanli. Terrified of losing his throne to his exiled brother, the Pasha abandoned his exorbitant demands and sued for peace. On June fourth, eighteen-five, a treaty was signed on board the frigate USS Constitution in Tripoli harbor. The Pasha agreed to release all three hundred and seven American prisoners and formally renounced all future demands for tribute from the United States.
The First Barbary War was a transformative milestone for the young American republic. In defying the corsairs, Thomas Jefferson demonstrated to the crowned heads of Europe that the United States was neither an unprotected colonial outpost nor a paper republic willing to barter away its dignity. The conflict served as the great training ground for a generation of legendary naval officers—men like Stephen Decatur, Isaac Hull, and David Porter—who would prove vital seven years later during the War of eighteen-twelve against the greatest naval power on the globe.
By refusing to bow to extortion, Thomas Jefferson established a precedent that would define American foreign policy for two centuries: that free seas, sovereign commerce, and national honor are principles worth defending, no matter how distant the shore or how formidable the foe.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The First Barbary War proved to the world that the United States was capable of projecting power across the globe to defend its citizens and its principles. Stephen Decatur's nighttime raid and the Marines' march across the sands of Derne became foundational legends of the American military. Next week, we turn to America's fourth President, James Madison, and the harrowing moment in eighteen hundred and fourteen when an invading British army torched Washington, and a freak storm saved the nation's capital. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
